Helping is one thing; being officious about it is another.

No obeisance was required, only an accurate report.

A congenial room, three good arguments, and the afternoon gone.

An affable man who has never once told anyone what he thinks.
She is gregarious and the flat is never empty.
Gregarious by habit, he still writes best alone.
An urbane host who could keep three difficult guests apart.
The urbane surface never breaks, whatever is said to him.

Too ingenuous for the job, and everyone knew it but him.

The letter is artless and all the more convincing for it.
An artless remark, and the room went quiet.

A diffident knock, and then a very good question.

grammar.label: implicature — what is meant without being said
grammar.form: saying less than is relevant, so the hearer infers the rest
grammar.meaning: conveys a meaning the words do not carry and the speaker can deny

explanation.en: A reference that says only 'His attendance was punctual' says something devastating without a word of criticism. The hearer reasons: if there were more to say, she would have said it. This is how English does most of its unpleasantness, and it is entirely deniable, which is the point.
explanation.uz: 'His attendance was punctual' degan tavsiyanoma bir og'iz tanqidsiz halokatli narsa aytadi. Tinglovchi shunday fikr yuritadi: aytadigan ko'proq narsa bo'lsa, aytilardi.

grammar.positive_example: Asked about the second candidate, she said he had always been punctual.
grammar.negative_example: Asked about the second candidate, she said he was punctual and also incompetent.

l1_notes.uz: Ingliz tilida noxush narsalarning katta qismi shu yo'l bilan aytiladi; to'g'ridan-to'g'ri tarjima uni butunlay yo'qotadi.

grammar.label: the grammar of politeness at a distance
grammar.form: the more indirect the form, the greater the imposition it acknowledges
grammar.meaning: matches the shape of a request to how much it costs the hearer

explanation.en: 'Pass the salt' and 'I wonder whether you might possibly be able to pass the salt' are both grammatical; one is normal and the other is sarcasm. English scales indirectness to imposition, so a small request in elaborate wording reads as cold or as mockery. The error learners make is not rudeness but excess.
explanation.uz: 'Pass the salt' va 'I wonder whether you might possibly…' — ikkalasi ham to'g'ri, biri odatiy, ikkinchisi kinoya. Ingliz tili bilvositalikni iltimosning og'irligiga moslaydi.

grammar.positive_example: Could you send the file when you have a moment?
grammar.negative_example: I was wondering whether you might conceivably find it possible to send the file.

l1_notes.uz: O'zbek tilida hurmat shakllari grammatik; ingliz tilida ular bilvositalik darajasi bilan beriladi va ortiqchasi zarar qiladi.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Kamola asked me for a reference for a man I cannot recommend.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'His attendance was punctual and his files were always in order.'

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Every word of it. And anyone who reads it will know exactly what I think.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Because of what I could have said and did not. She asked about his judgement and I answered about his files.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: It is honest and it is not brave. The brave letter says the thing.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: Why not write the brave letter?

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Because he will read it one day, and because I am not certain enough to put it on paper. That is the real reason and I should admit it.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: Your reply to the ministry is very formal.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: I have never met them. Distance and formality go together: the further away the reader, the more work the politeness has to do.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: With Kamola you write four words.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: With Kamola four words is politeness. Fifteen would be an insult.
